definition: Oligarchic means ruled or controlled by a small group of people.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word oligarchic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know oligarchic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The debate league is quietly oligarchic: three coaches write the rules, pick the judges, and decide which schools may join.
Elitist attitudes merely favor a polished few — milder than oligarchic, where the few have stopped being favorites and started being the government.
Autocratic goes further than oligarchic along the narrowing road of power: the small circle shrinks to a single ruler holding everything.

Clannish means run like a closed family circle, cool to outsiders — loyalty flows to kin and long-timers, and newcomers stay strangers for years. Oligarchic is about power rather than warmth: a small group actually rules. A clannish shop can be friendly inside and powerless; an oligarchic one holds the wheel.

Clubby describes coziness among insiders — nicknames, standing favors, the same faces at the same table. Oligarchic adds the part an analyst cares about: the insiders hold actual power and write the rules for everyone else. A clubby office is merely irritating; an oligarchic one is governed by its clique.

Oligarchic means ruled or controlled by a small group of people.
On paper the fishing cooperative has ninety members; in practice it is oligarchic, run by the four families who own the boats, set the prices, and fill every seat on the disputes committee.
Oligarchic is more precise than 'unfair' or 'corrupt' because it names a shape of power: a small group holds it.
The group can be honest or crooked, rich or merely entrenched — what makes rule oligarchic is how few hands are on the wheel.
Oligarchic is analysis, not just insult: it claims power sits with a small circle, whatever the letterhead says.
Its unit-mates split hairs that essays love — plutocratic tells you the few are the rich, theocratic that the rulers are religious authorities, meritocratic that rank was earned.
When the only fact you have is 'a handful rules,' oligarchic is the honest choice.

When the Palm Street pool association posted its summer rules, half the neighborhood learned that lap lanes now close to children after four o'clock.
No one remembered voting on it, because no vote had happened.

The association is oligarchic in everything but name: three founding households hold the treasurer's box, the schedule, and the key to the pump room, and the annual meeting exists to announce what they have already decided.
They are pleasant people, quick with a wave from their matching deck chairs.
But pleasantness is beside the point when eighty member families have exactly as much say as the pool's inflatable swan.
